Home shows a Today card for the next meal slot, picked from local time and the family schedule, with one primary suggestion and two alternates.
Swiping a card left shows the next candidate; swiping right accepts it. Accepting creates a planned meal and, if enabled, a Cook Card (M4).
Context chips above the card: Low energy, Quick (<20 min), Guests, Rainy/Cold (auto from weather), Sick-day light food, Sunday special, Use leftovers. Each chip re-ranks immediately.
Ask box (text or voice): natural-language constraints such as "something with paneer, no onion, under 30 minutes". The LLM turns this into filters and weights; the ranker still makes the choice.
Familiar ↔ Adventurous dial (0–100) sets how many never-cooked catalogue dishes can appear. Default 20.
A "Why this?" tap shows the top three score drivers in plain language.
Home-screen widget (Android and iOS) shows the Today card with Accept and Next.

What's available: a strip of vegetable chips (seasonal, from the family's usual buys) plus recorded leftovers. Ticking what's in the kitchen boosts dishes that use them. Two further options always show: "Order a missing item" (Blinkit) and "Order in" (Zomato).

Family with members; each member has a role (Planner, Cook, Eater, Shopper), an age band (toddler, child, teen, adult, senior) and optional WhatsApp number. Age sets defaults: milder spice and smaller portions for young children, softer and lighter food for seniors.
Hard rules per member: diet (veg, egg, non-veg, vegan, Jain, satvik), exclusions (onion-garlic, specific ingredients), allergies, spice tolerance.

Day rules: recurring (no meat on Tuesdays), lunar calendar fasts (Ekadashi, Pradosh), festival windows (Navratri, Ramzan, Shravan), each tied to members. The system ships a preloaded panchang calendar that the family can edit.

One base, many plates: when rules conflict, suggest a base dish with per-member variants (for example sabudana khichdi for the fasting member, a regular version for others) and show who each plate is for.
Onboarding takes under 2 minutes: family name, members, rules, and "pick 10 dishes you make often" from a regional catalogue, used as cold-start history.
Catalogue packs at launch: North Indian, South Indian and General (pan-India), with local dish names and aliases. More regions come later.

Create family: any user can create a family and becomes its first Planner. Others join with a signed, expiring invite link (app or WhatsApp). A person can belong to more than one family (for example parents' home).

Free-text preferences in English, for the family or one member: "prefer healthier options", "less spicy for kids", "no maida on weekdays". The LLM turns each into a visible soft rule (a weight on tags such as fried, spice, millet) that the user can edit or delete. Preferences never override hard rules.

Voice log using free on-device speech recognition (Android and iOS cover Hindi, English and major Indic languages), including code-mixed speech ("aaj dinner mein rajma chawal aur raita"): parsed into dishes, slot and date, confirmed with one tap.
Photo log: the image model suggests the dish names; the user confirms. The April photo flow stays but becomes optional.
Auto-log: an accepted plan becomes a cooked meal after its slot ends unless the user changes it. A 9 pm digest lists anything unconfirmed.
Cook photos sent back over WhatsApp attach to the planned meal as proof and log it.
Quick-reuse chips show the last 8 distinct dishes for one-tap logging.

Cook Card: when the Planner confirms a day's meals, the app opens WhatsApp with the card pre-filled for the cook's chat (click-to-chat or share sheet, free). A reminder fires at a set time (default 9:30 pm the day before) if the card hasn't been sent.
The card is in the cook's language and script, with an optional voice note generated by the phone's free on-device text-to-speech and attached as audio.
Quantities scale to headcount (for example "rice 2 cups, dal 1 cup for 5 people") from catalogue portion metadata; per-member variants are called out.

The card carries a link to a no-login Cook page (signed link, free static hosting). The cook taps OK, Missing item or Change dish there. "Missing item" feeds the M6 list; "Change" shows the Planner two alternates.
The cook's repertoire: dishes the cook knows are tagged; suggestions favour them when the cook is scheduled.
Cook schedule (days, slots, leave) sets which slots produce Cook Cards.

Prioritised choices: per slot the Planner can approve up to 3 ranked options (1st, 2nd, backup). The cook picks the highest one she can make with what's available and taps it on the Cook page. A "standing menu bank" of pre-approved dishes lets the cook choose on days the Planner doesn't plan.
Family vote: the planner shares 2–3 options to the family WhatsApp group as a vote link (free web page); it closes at a set time and the winner is planned.
Kid mode: a picture-card swipe on the planner's phone ("Yum / Meh"), with no account needed.
Tiffin return check: a notification after school pick-up asks "How did the tiffin come back?" (Empty, Half, Full). This is a strong acceptance signal per child.
Quick reactions after a meal (Loved it, OK, Not again) per member; the April feedback chips map onto these.
After logging, "Anything left over?" records the leftover dish and a rough amount.

Leftover chains: the catalogue holds transformations (dal to dal paratha, rice to lemon rice, sabzi to frankie). Leftovers boost linked dishes for the next 1–2 slots. What the family actually did with each leftover is recorded and learned (section 8).
Staples, not inventory: the family ticks about 25 staples it keeps; the system assumes they are there unless marked out. No item-level stock tracking.

Blinkit cart handoff: for planned meals, list ingredients not in staples, merge them with the cook's "Missing item" taps, and open Blinkit with a search per item (deep link), or share the list to Zepto, Instamart or WhatsApp. Moves to a cart API if a partnership becomes possible.
A monthly "food saved" counter based on leftover chains used.

Order in with Zomato: when the family picks "Order in", the app suggests 3 dishes that fit the day's rules and recent pattern (for example "no North Indian for 3 days") and opens Zomato with a search. The order is logged as a meal so the history stays complete.
Tomorrow plan push at a time the user sets (default 9 pm): tomorrow's breakfast, tiffins and lunch suggestions, confirmed in one tap.

7-day family calendar: a week grid (days × slots, one row per tiffin per child) where meals can be pinned, dragged and swapped; unpinned slots fill with live suggestions. Rules, fasts, festivals, guests and school holidays show on the calendar. The week can be shared to WhatsApp as an image.

Occasion planner: event name, date, guest list (named guest groups), headcount and rules. It builds a menu of starter, main, bread or rice, sweet, and avoids dishes served to the same guest group before.
Life modes that change ranking for a date range: Exam week (light, familiar), Travel (pause), Guests staying, Recovery (light food), Festival.
Festival packs (Diwali, Onam, Pongal, Eid, Christmas, Durga Puja) offered 7 days ahead, based on the family's region and calendar.

Two tiffins per child: each school-going child can have a short-break box (small, dry, finger food) and a lunch box. Both are suggested as a pair, kept distinct from each other and from breakfast, and planned the evening before. School days and holidays come from a per-child school calendar.
Each catalogue dish carries food-group tags: cereal, millet, pulse, vegetable, green leafy, dairy, egg or meat, fried.
Balance rings show the week against simple targets based on ICMR-NIN 2024 (for example pulses at least 5 days, green leafy at least 3, millets at least 2, fried at most 2). No calories.
Ranking adds a small boost for a group that is behind ("No greens since Monday"). The household can switch this off.
Timeline history grouped by date with thumbnails, member filters and search. This closes the April gaps.
Family favourites shelf built automatically from repeated positive outcomes, with a "safe choice" badge.
Heirloom recipes: record a voice note (for example Nani explaining her sambar), stored with transcript and linked to the dish.
Monthly and yearly "Year in food" recap (most-loved dish, new dishes tried, leftovers saved), shareable as an image.
Every suggestion has a reason string built from its top drivers.
Hide dish (forever or for 30 days); pause learning; reset recommendations.
Consent: each member's WhatsApp number is added only after they opt in via a link; the cook can opt out from the Cook page.
Export the household's data (JSON or CSV) and delete it within 30 days, in line with India's DPDP Act.
